 Main content Elections Pa. election 2026: How to vote, where to vote, and everything you need to know for Nov. 3
 by
 Elizabeth Estrada of Spotlight PA 
 |
 Oct. 26, 2026 
 Matt Smith / For Spotlight PA Share:
 HARRISBURG — Pennsylvania’s 2026 general election is quickly approaching. If you still have questions about where your polling place is, who is on the ballot, and how to vote, Spotlight PA has you covered.
 On Tuesday, Nov. 3, voters across the commonwealth will cast their ballots for governor and lieutenant governor, along with the entire Pennsylvania House and half of the state Senate. All of Pennsylvania’s 17 congressional districts will also be up for election. There may be local ballot questions, depending where you live.
 Before you submit your ballot, here’s a last-minute checklist of everything you’ll need to vote.
 First, the basics:
 Make sure you’re registered. If you aren’t, it is unfortunately too late to register to vote in the upcoming election — the deadline was Oct. 19. You can check your voter registration status on the Pennsylvania Department of State website .
 The deadline to request a mail or absentee ballot is Oct. 27. Your county election office has to receive your application by 5 p.m. that day. If you have already applied for a mail ballot, you can track it on the Pennsylvania Department of State's election ballot status webpage . To be counted, your mail ballot must be received by your county election office by 8 p.m. on Election Day. Read more about mail ballots and how to properly fill them out .
 If you plan to vote in person, you can find your polling place online .
 You need to bring a form of ID such as a driver’s license or a passport if it’s your first time voting at your polling location. You can find the full list of acceptable IDs on Pennsylvania's official election website .
 Whether you’re voting in person or by mail, here’s everything you need to know about your Election Day voting rights.
 For general voting and election resources, check out Spotlight PA’s 2026 Election Center .
 Still have questions? You can reach out to your county election office for answers. Find contact information for your county on the Pennsylvania election website .
 Here’s what you can expect to see on your ballot:
 In the race for governor , voters will choose between Democratic incumbent Josh Shapiro, Republican state treasurer Stacy Garrity, and Libertarian Ken Krawchuk. Each gubernatorial candidate is running alongside a candidate for lieutenant governor . Take our quiz to see which major party candidate for governor most closely aligns with what matters to you, and use this tool to see how much money Shapiro and Garrity have raised for their campaigns.
 Aside from statewide races, the races and candidates on your ballot will depend on where you live. You may be able to find a sample ballot on your official county website, which you can locate using the Pennsylvania Department of State voting and election webpage .
 All of Pennsylvania’s 17 congressional districts are on the ballot this year. Use this tool to find your district and check out our guide that covers all of the races, including the three that could determine which party controls the U.S. House for the next two years.
 The entire Pennsylvania House and half the state Senate are on the ballot this year. Learn which races could determine control of the Pennsylvania General Assembly and check out Spotlight PA’s guide to vetting candidates to help you evaluate which candidates you want to send to or keep in Harrisburg.
 There are no statewide ballot measures in November, but some voters may see local questions — for instance, Allegheny County and Philadelphia both have them. Check your county’s election website or sample ballot to learn exactly which races, candidates, and questions you will be voting for.
 Read Spotlight PA’s complete coverage, including candidate and election guides, and more, at our 2026 Election Center .

 Before you go, a request for help...
 We grant elected officials extraordinary power when we give them our vote, which means we must demand extraordinary accountability once they are in office. But that’s impossible if “We the People” don’t have information about what decisions they’re making and how they spend our money.
 That’s why Spotlight PA exists, but we can’t keep digging without your support.
 We’re independent, we live here, and we don’t answer to shareholders or a big corporation. We’re unbiased in this polarized time, with no political agenda or opinion pieces. And we’re a nonprofit, which means we prioritize in-depth investigative and public-service reporting that puts you first.
 Uncertain times call for decisive action. More than 11,000 readers just like you — friends and neighbors in your community who still give a damn about truth, accountability, and transparency — are standing behind the free and fearless reporting Spotlight PA provides. Join them now by making a gift and ensuring this work can continue. 
 Thank you!
